subject: grayWolf
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: gray wolf standing alert.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning the proportions for a Warcraft-style gray wolf model—chunky and exaggerated with heavy shoulders and big paws, roughly 0.8m shoulder height and 1.3m body length, scaled up slightly bulkier than a realistic wolf.

Mapping out the skeleton structure next: hips as root joint, spine chains running forward to the chest and neck, a tail chain going backward, with leg chains parented to the hips and spine. I'm working through specific joint coordinates for an alert standing pose—head raised, ears up, tail straight back—placing hips, shoulders, neck, and head positions in 3D space before starting the body loft.

Writing loft parameters...

Still structuring spine joints...

To avoid a zero-length hips bone, I'll offset the root so pelvis-to-spine1 and pelvis-to-tail1 both have real length, naming the root "hips" with spine starting slightly forward and tail starting slightly back.

Now I'm working out the leg positions and joint chains — shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw for the front legs — deciding to hand-write the segments directly rather than relying on a generic limb helper for better control.

Four joints give three spans plus the paw tip, so I can sweep a tube through that chain with tapering radii from shoulder to wrist. For the chunky stylized look, I'll add a sphere blob at the shoulder for bulk and build the paw as its own rounded part with small toe capsules and claws.

Now I'm placing the rear leg joints — hip, stifle (knee, swung forward), hock (swung back), and metatarsal down to the paw — mimicking real wolf hind-leg geometry, and sketching coordinates for each point before chaining them into a limb sweep.

Checking the paw sphere's bottom doesn't clip below ground within tolerance, then moving to the tail: building a drooping chain of points from the rump down and back to suggest a relaxed, alert posture.

For textures I'm planning a modest set of 5-12 assets: an amber wolf-eye decal, gray fur tuft cards with dark tips for the neck ruff and chest mane, cream-colored tufts for the cheek ruffs, and considering a Warcraft-style emblem to add character flair.

Deciding to keep this a pure wolf rather than adding war paint or a collar, I'm leaning into exaggerated features instead -- a huge scruff mane, heavy brows, big fangs, jagged fur tufts, chunky paws, and glowing amber eyes. I'll also need a dark nose texture with small sphere nostrils, a fur-gradient inner ear texture using paint, and a fur streak decal.

I'm planning dark saddle markings on the flanks via paint, plus face markings like a dark mask around the eyes and whisker dots on the muzzle, a fur spike card for the back ridge, and a jagged fur ruff for the shoulders. Now I'm setting up the color palette with gray coat tones, dark and light contrast shades, cream and tan accents, black, a dark nose color, bone-colored claws, and amber eyes.

Adding mouth and coat colors...

Still writing coat shader logic...

Still defining coat zones...

Now I'm working out the head and neck chain positions in model space, placing a sequence of joints from the shoulders up through the neck to the head base to get an alert, forward-leaning wolf posture.

Figuring out head dimensions and orientation: setting the skull and muzzle proportions larger for a Warcraft-style look, and positioning the head joint with local forward/up/right axes so rotation stays intuitive regardless of orientation.

I realize the world-direction offsets are measured relative to the frame's aim, not the head's own tilt, so I'll keep the head joint essentially level to avoid mismatches, with maybe a slight downward dir like [0,-0.08,1]. The jaw joint can stay closed with a similar near-level orientation, though I'm considering whether a slight open mouth reads better for the pose.

I'm deciding to keep the jaw closed but add visible fangs protruding below the upper lip for that Warcraft-style tusked look, rather than actually opening the mouth. Now I'm sketching the skull geometry -- a scaled sphere positioned at the head joint for the cranium -- and weighing smooth versus flat shading, landing on smooth for the body with flat shading reserved for decorative bits, before moving on to building the muzzle as a frustum shape.

Writing loft station coordinates...

Adding fangs and incisors on the jawbone, then setting up eye decals positioned on the skull surface...

I need to figure out which eye corner faces inward vs outward for correct mirroring: for the model's left eye seen on the viewer's right, the inner corner faces viewer's left, so I'll mirror the texture for s=-1 while keeping s=1 unmirrored, using default world-up orientation for the decal.

Instead of trying to compute the exact surface point manually, I realize I can use the surface's `around(center).at(azimuth, elevation)` approach like the kit example does, placing the eye at roughly azimuth s*50, elevation 18 on the skull ellipsoid—this should give a robust hit point for the decal projection.

For the brow ridge, I'm thinking of sweeping a small rod shape between two surface hit points near the eyes, lifted slightly outward to suggest a scowling brow.

For ears, I'm planning erect, rounded triangular shapes like a wolf's but scaled up for a Warcraft-style look, extruding the outline along the head's surface direction.

Working out ear thickness direction for the mirrored side, then planning to build ears as two layered extrusions: an outer gray shell and a smaller lighter inner piece offset slightly forward for a cream/pink-gray inner-ear look.

Now I'm sketching the ear outline shape with sharp points and bevel/thickness values, considering adding small fur tuft cards around the ear base, and attaching the ear to the head bone. I'm also computing where on the skull surface the ear should sit by solving for the skull's ellipsoid radius at the chosen forward/up/left offsets.

For the signature shaggy cheek ruffs and neck mane, I'm thinking through two approaches: scattering fur cards across the cheeks and neck sweep, or arranging rings of jagged blade shapes at multiple neck levels — I'll likely combine both for a fuller effect.

I'm now working out the tuft texture itself: rather than giving each card a flat color, I want a grayscale gradient texture (dark to light at the root) that gets tinted by sampling the coat color paint at each root point, so the fur naturally blends into the body's color scheme.

I'm worried using paint tints per-card could blow up the atlas with too many flat colors, so I should stick to a handful of tints (gray mid, dark, light, cream) across separate cards calls to stay within mesh/texture limits. The documentation itself uses a paint color with cards, so this approach should be supported.

For textures, I'm planning amber eyes, two tuft variants (long jagged and short wide, picked randomly), a muzzle decal with whisker dots and a lip line, and fur-strand texture for ear interiors -- though I need to check whether extrudes accept textures or only paints, since the ear shape is built via extrusion.

I'm also adding a dark fur-blade texture for the spine ridge and a fluffy cross-card texture for the tail, bringing the total to about five or six textures. For extra character I want to include a battle scar decal (pink-white scar lines) on the shoulder or muzzle, plus a notch cut into the left ear outline for a war-torn look.

Now I'm working out the part budget, aiming for 180-340 total parts: one loft each for body, neck, and tail, four leg sweeps, two shoulder and two haunch blobs, then four paws each with eight small parts for toes and claws (32 total). For the head I'm planning a skull, muzzle, jaw, nose, nostrils, lips, roughly ten teeth, two eye decals, two brow shapes, several ear parts, and cheek ruff cards, skipping the tongue since the mouth stays closed.

I'm deciding to keep the jaw closed for an alert wolf expression but letting small fangs peek out for a bit of menace. For fur, I'm sketching about eight card calls across the neck mane, chest, back ridge, tail, leg feathering, and cheeks, plus a jagged spiked ruff around the neck built from three rings of ten spikes each, and I'm considering adding whisker rods on each cheek to push the part count up toward 150 or more, along with dorsal ridge cards running along the spine path.

Writing spike placement logic...

That confirms loft uses sweep under the hood, so I'll use that for the body shape. Now I'm sketching out the body stations from rump to chest, defining the center position, width, and height at each z-coordinate along the torso.

Adjusting the chest station to lower the withers height to around 0.93, which brings total body height to roughly 1.45 once the neck and ears are stacked on top—a reasonably chunky Warcraft-scale proportion.

Now plotting the spine joint chain along the back centerline with hip, spine1-4, and tail connections, then starting the neck path curving upward from the shoulders toward the skull position.

The neck arcs up to the head joint, with the head extending forward so the nose sits well beyond the body—making this wolf roughly 2.45m nose-to-tail, bigger than a real wolf but fitting a Warcraft-style exaggerated creature.

Rechecking proportions, I decide to tighten the body range so the total length comes closer to 2.1m with a shoulder height around 0.92, still generously sized but less sprawling. Now I'm reworking the final coordinates—setting the hip root position and laying out the spine points along the z-axis.

I'm defining body loft stations with y/z centers and width/height values to shape the torso cross-sections, then placing neck joints curving up to the head position, with neck radii tapering and a chain of neck bones leading to the skull center placed forward and up.

For the legs, I'm setting shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joint positions down the front limb with tapering sweep radii, parented to the last spine joint for proper attachment.

Then the paw itself gets a scaled sphere at the foot position, with four small toe spheres fanned across the front of the paw and tiny forward-pointing claw cones at their tips.

Now I'm working out the hind leg joint chain—hip, knee, hock, and paw—mirroring the naming pattern used for the front legs (shoulder/elbow/wrist/paw) but with side-specific suffixes to keep every joint name unique.

Positioning the thigh mass sphere and hind paw sphere, tracking radii that taper from hip to hock, then starting the tail chain rooted at the hips.

Setting up the neck chain with catmull smoothing too, then defining head joints and a jaw joint parented to the head with its own aim and role.

Checking the neck-to-skull transition radii and positions to make sure the geometries overlap cleanly, then moving to head coloring logic with a nested paint function distinguishing the muzzle zone by its z-coordinate.

Still blending head shading...

Still writing coat shading...

I'm adding a dark streak down the front of the forelegs like a gray wolf's leg stripe, plus fur-tuft cards scattered along the back of each leg for feathering detail, with each leg getting its own mesh call. Now I'm moving on to designing the tuft texture shape as a jagged blade SVG.

Adjusting stroke width to 1.6 for proper scaling, then sketching a second wider flame-tufted variant and starting on eye shape designs...

Designing the slanted almond eye with an arched dark lid outline, amber iris gradient, round pupil, and a small highlight, clipped to the almond shape.

Still writing eye shapes and scar texture details...

For the muzzle, I'm drawing whisker pore dots as a texture and placing it as a decal on the upper muzzle sides via a surface loft, positioning it near the muzzle surface with appropriate orientation and sizing.

Now I'm setting up the neck mane as fur cards scattered across a neck surface, filtering out the underside, with flow direction angled back and down, lean around 60 degrees, and sized appropriately for a mane look.

For the chest I'm scattering cream-colored tuft cards filtered to the front z-region, hanging downward with their own flow and lean angles for a bib-like appearance. I'm also planning a ring of stylized spike blades around the neck base to create a Warcraft-style shoulder ruff.

Still writing spike parameters...

For tail fluff I'm scattering cards along the sweep using the tail coat paint gradient, and considering whether this wolf needs extra Warcraft-style details like worn rope bits (probably not). I'm also planning finer facial details: eyebrow ridges, nostrils, lips, teeth, whiskers, cheek cards, ear tufts, notches, and claws.

For the eye glow, I'll apply the glow effect to the eye decal at a strength around 0.9 so it reads as a bright amber Warcraft-style eye regardless of scene lighting, then set up a reusable fur helper and start importing the builder modules I need, including the glow kit.

Setting up the builder config...

Defining the spine chain with a curve through the body...

Then I'm setting up the body loft, referencing the bone chain from hips through spine to head for shaping the mesh.

Now I'm defining the neck chain, parenting it to the end of the spine, then adding the head joint with its position and direction. I'm also creating a sweep tube for the neck using a tapering radius profile.

Next I'm setting up the tail chain parented to the hips, sweeping it with a radius profile that tapers at both ends, and assigning its coat color.

Now I'm building leg chains for each side, naming joints like shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw, parented to the spine for the front legs.

Still placing geometry...

Now mapping the hind leg structure: hip joint chain feeding the thigh mass, hock fur tufts, and hind paw placement with toes and claws positioned slightly forward compared to the front paws. I'm noting the coat sweep coloring applies to both front and hind legs before moving on to the head parts function.

Building the skull with a smooth sphere, lofting the muzzle through tapering cross-sections out to the nose tip, and adding a small glossy nose with a highlight sphere before starting on the nostril detail.

Now I'm working out the lower jaw as a lofted shape with its own cream coat color, aligning its top edge with the bottom contour of the muzzle so the mouth closes naturally.

Now I'm tracing the mouth line sweep across both sides, matching it against the muzzle's half-width at each station so the lip curve stays tucked just inside the muzzle contour with a small corner radius.

I'll snap the mouth line to the muzzle surface alone since the rough points sit lower, letting it ride the head bone naturally at the seam. For teeth, I'm positioning the upper fangs as spikes rooted at the muzzle's bottom edge, angled slightly inward and downward with ivory coloring, though I need to nail down the exact base height.

Working through the lower fangs' placement, I realize their tips would actually tuck inside the closed upper muzzle, which is fine since they stay hidden while the upper fangs remain visible — I'll also add a small row of tiny incisor cones near the front of the muzzle.

Now I'm skipping the tongue and inner mouth detail and moving on to the brows, which I'm positioning using angular offsets around the skull surface relative to the eye socket location, sweeping a curved ridge above each eye using a catmull spline through frame-adjusted points.

Then I'm placing the eyes using similar angular hit-testing on the skull surface, decaling the eye texture with mirrored orientation depending on which side of the head it's on, while working out how the eye slant should read correctly for the model's left versus right side given the viewer's perspective.

matching viewer's left, so no mirror is needed when drawn with the inner corner positioned at the low-x side—since decals project to read undistorted from the front using the hit normal as direction, this should work fine. For sizing, I'll make the eyes slightly bigger than the base scale—around 0.085×0.054—to get that bigger Warcraft-style eye look relative to the skull width.

I'm defining the quad decals for the glowing eyes on the curved skull surface, applying a glow effect, and leaving the dark eye-line markings baked into the texture rather than separate geometry. For the ears, I'm sketching outline points for a battle-worn look, adding a small V-shaped notch cut into the outer edge of one ear using sharp-cornered points while being careful the outline doesn't self-intersect.

Deciding on zero smoothing for a faceted low-poly ear look, and working out the ear's tilt and placement coordinates relative to the bone head.

The outline axis stays outward on both left and right ears despite the mirroring, with the notch only appearing on the right ear. I'm cross-multiplying the axis vectors to confirm which direction the ear's thickness should extend, getting a forward +Z result for the left ear and checking the mirrored case.

For the inner ear detail, I need to offset it slightly forward of the ear's front face (by about 0.011, given the ear is 0.02 thick) and figure out the correct placement position accounting for the base offsets and mirror sign.

Writing inner ear outline and gradient paint...

Adding cheek fur tufts and planning whisker rods extending outward and backward from the muzzle sides.

Using a ray cast against the body surface to find the scar hit point, then placing the decal there with a slight roll for a natural look. I want to give the wolf that heavy Warcraft feel with a thick shoulder fur ruff and mane, plus warm tan-cream color accents against the cool blue-gray base, skipping mud/snow details. For the tail, I'm scattering fur tuft cards along the tail tube with scattered positions and a downward-back flow direction for texture.

I'm darkening the tail tip and underside using a smoothstep blend toward a darker tone based on height, plus a subtle dark streak along the top ridge. Now I'm tallying up the texture atlas -- eye, fur tufts, scar, and whisker marks -- and figuring out how to handle tinted variations of the same texture (like a darker ridge tuft) without blowing up the texture count, deciding to use procedural paint tints for the mane and tail coat instead of separate texture entries.

I'm also considering adding a decal texture for fur flicks -- small clusters of dark pointed strokes scattered across the flanks and shoulders -- to add painterly surface detail, planning to place these decals at several points around the body's sides and haunches using directional placement based on body bounding box center.

Writing SVG code...

I need to work out the decal's "up" direction so the fur flicks point backward toward the tail with a slight downward tilt, rather than straight up.

Mud at feet and snow are already handled. Now I want to add jagged Warcraft-style details: a cream chest bib, and a ring of jagged spike blades around the cheeks/skull sides angled back-down to look like a spiky ruff.

Still placing spikes...

Now I'm building a dorsal ridge by sampling points along the body tube and feeding them into cards with downward-tilted flow and dark green coloring, then doing similar ridge sampling along the neck sweep.

Adding chunkier Warcraft-style details now: a thicker ring ruff at the neck/shoulders, extra brow and snout wrinkles, and a jaw joint with lower jaw spikes positioned relative to the head.

I'm scattering small cream tufts on the jaw surface, skipping the tongue, and double-checking that paws, toes, and claws sit flush with the floor without clipping -- verifying the leg sweeps and paw spheres align so the lowest point of the model rests right at ground level.

Now I'm mapping out the front leg joints from shoulder to paw, finding the segments a bit too thin for the chunky style, so I'm bumping up the radii at each joint to give it a sturdier, more Warcraft-like look while checking that the leg width doesn't awkwardly clip into the torso's chest sides.

For the hind leg, I'm placing the hip, knee, hock, and paw joints and checking the haunch bulge sits properly within the body bounds, then measuring segment distances and comparing the knee's forward position against the belly line to make sure the leg silhouette reads correctly.

For the head, I'm setting skull, muzzle, and nose positions and checking the head sits forward of the chest cap so it doesn't collide with the body front.

Now I'm working through the mane ring spikes along the neck curve, tilting each spike so it leans back toward the shoulders rather than forward, with radius and spike length tapering from the base of the neck to the head.

I'll keep the mane palette small to stay under the color limit, cycling a couple flat hex shades for variation. Then I'm sketching a small whisker-pore decal mark for the muzzle, a cluster of dark dots placed on both sides mirrored for symmetry.

I'm double-checking a few API assumptions before committing: decal targets should accept the skull part directly, Hit.moved offsets convert cleanly into frame points for the catmull curve, and part scale options likely take either a number or a vector, so I should bake scaling into the geometry itself to be safe.

Defining ellipsoid geometry helper...
